How to Soothe a Teething Baby: Safe Remedies That Work

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To soothe a teething baby, offer something cold and firm to chew: a solid rubber teething ring chilled in the fridge, a clean damp washcloth from the refrigerator, or a gentle gum massage with a clean finger. Extra feeds and cuddles cover the rest of most days, and a properly dosed pain reliever can back you up on the genuinely rough ones. Just as important is knowing what to skip, because several popular remedies carry real safety warnings.

Cold and pressure do most of the work

Cold plus gentle pressure is the combination that eases sore gums most reliably. Chill a solid rubber teething ring in the refrigerator, not the freezer. A ring frozen solid becomes hard enough to bruise the gums, and extreme cold can hurt more than it helps. Let your baby gnaw at their own pace while you stay nearby, and wash the ring with soap and water after each session. If your baby has started solids, some parents offer chilled soft foods in a mesh or silicone feeder, which adds cold and chewing at the same time; stay within arm's reach and watch closely, since food is involved. Rotate two or three rings through the fridge so a cool one is always ready.

A clean, damp washcloth chilled in the refrigerator works almost as well and costs nothing. Wet one corner, chill it for twenty to thirty minutes, and let your baby chew the cold end while you hold the rest. Some babies like a knot tied in the middle for extra texture. Gum massage is the other free tool: wash your hands, then rub the sore spot with firm, slow circles using one finger. The counterpressure feels good against a tooth pushing up from below. Many babies fight it for a few seconds and then lean into it. Try it before feeds if a sore mouth is making nursing or bottles frustrating.

Comfort beyond the mouth

Teething pain rises and falls in waves, and comfort from you often matters as much as anything you put in the mouth. Offer extra feeds if your baby wants them, since sucking is soothing on its own and a snuggly feed calms the whole body, not just the gums. Carrying, rocking, a walk outside, or a warm bath can all shift a fussy stretch. Distraction is legitimate medicine at this age: a new texture to grab, a song, a change of room. You are not spoiling a baby by comforting them through a sore few days. Extra clinginess during teething is normal, and it passes.

Heavy drool deserves its own routine, because a raw chin can bother a baby as much as the gums do. Pat the chin and neck dry gently through the day rather than rubbing. A thin layer of plain barrier cream or petroleum jelly protects the skin, and a soft cotton bib changed when it gets soggy keeps the chest dry. Take the bib off for sleep and skip loose cloths in the crib; a quick chin dry and a little barrier cream at bedtime is enough. For babies older than about six months, sips of cold water from a cup with meals can soothe the mouth too.

Pain medicine, used honestly

Medicine has a real place on the genuinely rough days, and it works better when the rules are clear. Acetaminophen, sold as Tylenol in North America, can generally be used from around 2 to 3 months of age. Confirm the dose with your pediatrician or pharmacist before the first use and again as your baby grows, because infant dosing is based on current weight and the labels on products for children under 2 say to ask a doctor. Ibuprofen, sold as Advil or Motrin, is an option from about 6 months. Always use the dosing syringe that comes with the product rather than a kitchen spoon, and write down the time of each dose so a tired brain does not double up.

Save medicine for the days and nights that are clearly bad, not as a routine for the whole teething season. A tooth that is actively cutting through usually hurts for a few days at a time, so weeks of scheduled doses suggest something else is going on and is worth a call to your clinician. Never give aspirin to a baby or child, and do not rub any medicine directly on the gums. If you are unsure whether a dose is due, how much to give, or whether teething is really the cause, a pharmacist or your pediatric office can answer quickly. Asking is normal.

The remedies to skip

Some popular products are not just unhelpful, they carry real warnings. The FDA advises against benzocaine teething gels and liquids, including Orajel, for children under 2 because benzocaine can cause a rare but serious blood problem called methemoglobinemia, which reduces the oxygen the blood carries. The numbing also washes away with drool within minutes, so the risk buys almost no relief. Homeopathic teething tablets have drawn FDA warnings as well, after some were found to contain inconsistent amounts of belladonna. Prescription lidocaine products are not for teething either. If a gel or tablet promises to numb the gums, put it back on the shelf.

Amber teething necklaces look gentle but are not. The American Academy of Pediatrics warns against them because a necklace on a baby is a strangulation risk, especially during sleep, and loose beads are a choking hazard. There is also no reliable evidence that amber releases anything pain relieving. Check the teethers themselves too: skip liquid filled rings, which can leak or burst if chewed hard or frozen, anything small enough to fit fully in the mouth, and toys with parts that can break off. One piece solid rubber or silicone teethers are the boring, safe choice. Boring is exactly what you want in something your baby chews all day.

A calm plan for teething nights

Nights are when teething pain feels loudest, partly because there is nothing else to think about. Build a short buffer before bed: a chilled teether or gum massage during the wind down, a full feed, and the same familiar routine as always. Keeping the routine matters, because babies settle faster inside a predictable pattern even on sore nights. When your baby wakes, start with the smallest comfort that works: a hand on the chest, a brief cuddle, a feed if it is due. Try not to build a brand new habit, like an hour of midnight play, that will outlast the tooth by months.

If a night is clearly miserable, a properly dosed pain reliever before bed is a reasonable backup, using the age rules and clinician confirmed dosing above. One honest reality check: teething can cause fussiness, drooling, and mildly warm temperatures, but a high fever, diarrhea, vomiting, or a baby who seems ill is not teething, so contact your clinician instead of waiting it out. It also helps to keep short notes on rough nights, new teeth, and any doses you gave; the BeMama app has a spot for dates, symptoms, and questions, which makes checkups faster. Most teething nights pass in a few days, and you will both sleep again.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Teething can cause gum discomfort, drooling, and a desire to chew, but it does not explain a true fever of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, marked lethargy, or significant illness. Cold (not frozen) teething items and gentle gum massage are common comfort measures.

Avoid products that create choking, strangulation, medication, or toxicity risks. Ask a pharmacist or child-health professional before using pain medicine or a topical product.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to note symptoms, temperature, sleep, and medicine instructions. Do not attribute fever or illness to teething based on the app.

When to seek help

Contact a clinician for fever, poor feeding, dehydration, breathing changes, or a child who seems unwell.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Fever and Your Baby
  • Public Health Agency of Canada — Make Your Home Safe for Your Child

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Cold and gentle pressure help most: a fridge chilled rubber ring, a cold damp washcloth, or a clean finger gum massage.
  • Chill teethers in the fridge, never the freezer, and choose solid one piece designs.
  • Save pain medicine for genuinely rough days, with dosing confirmed by your pediatrician or pharmacist.
  • Skip benzocaine gels like Orajel, homeopathic teething tablets, and amber teething necklaces.
  • A high fever or diarrhea points to illness, not teething, so contact your clinician.

Frequently asked questions

How can I help my teething baby sleep at night?

Offer a chilled teether or gum massage during the bedtime wind down, give a full feed, and keep the usual routine so your baby settles inside a familiar pattern. For night wakings, start with the smallest comfort that works before adding more. On a clearly bad night, a correctly dosed pain reliever is a reasonable backup once your pediatrician has confirmed the dose.

Are amber teething necklaces safe?

No. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises against amber teething necklaces because they create strangulation and choking risks, and there is no reliable evidence they relieve pain. A chilled rubber teether or a cold washcloth gives real relief without those risks.

Is baby Orajel safe for teething?

No. The FDA warns against benzocaine teething products like Orajel for children under 2 because benzocaine can cause a rare but serious blood condition, and the numbing washes away within minutes anyway. Use cold, pressure, and comfort instead, with an age appropriate pain reliever for the genuinely rough days.

When can I give Tylenol for teething?

Acetaminophen, sold as Tylenol, can generally be used for teething pain from around 2 to 3 months of age, with the dose confirmed by your pediatrician or pharmacist, since infant dosing is based on your baby's current weight and labels for children under 2 say to ask a doctor. Ibuprofen becomes an option from about 6 months. Keep medicine for the clearly bad days and nights rather than using it on a schedule for weeks.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
